bp: A short-video search engine is not just matching a query to clips. It is deciding what millions of people will see when they ask for something, including obscure requests that have very little past behavior attached to them. In those long-tail searches, the platform has weak evidence about which videos actually satisfy people. Kuaishou, according to the abstract, serves hundreds of millions of searches daily, so even a rare-query failure can affect many concrete viewing moments. The paper targets a rich-get-richer problem: videos that already received clicks get more chances to be shown, while good but underexposed videos remain hidden. Worse, sparse behavior can reward clickbait and shallow content because those videos may attract attention before users realize they are low quality. The system being built is therefore a search reranker that estimates likely user experience from the video content itself, not only from past clicks.
wh: The hard part is that the platform wants to rank by satisfaction, but the easiest evidence is user behavior, and behavior is both sparse and biased. A click says someone entered the video; it does not cleanly say the video was helpful, deep, trustworthy, or worth promoting. On popular queries, many interactions may average out some noise. On long-tail queries, there are too few observations, so one early burst of attention can become a lasting advantage. This is the Matthew effect named in the abstract: already exposed content keeps gaining evidence, while unseen content lacks the records needed to prove itself. Multimodal short videos add another difficulty because quality may live across frames, text, sound, and topic fit. A rule that counts clicks or surface query matches cannot see whether a video is shallow content dressed up with a tempting title. The paper must separate expected experience from exposure history.
naive: A smart beginner would rerank search results by past engagement: clicks, watches, likes, completion, or similar behavior signals. That seems natural because these signals come from real users rather than from guesses. The failure is that the signal is not evenly available. Long-tail queries have sparse user behavior, so the model has little chance to learn which niche videos are actually good. The beginner might then use popularity as a fallback, but popularity is partly caused by earlier ranking decisions. This turns the platform's old exposure pattern into the new quality estimate. Clickbait can win because it attracts quick behavior even when the viewing experience is poor, and high-quality videos with little exposure remain buried because the system never collects enough evidence about them.
ap: The paper's central move is to create a content-based experience scorer and use it during reranking. Instead of waiting for real user behavior on every candidate video, the method uses a large language model as a judge with broad prior knowledge, while also reading multimodal evidence from the video. The abstract describes two training stages. First, multimodal evidence is used to construct high-quality annotations for supervised fine-tuning, meaning the model is taught from labeled examples of what better experience looks like. Second, pairwise preference optimization teaches partial orderings among candidates, so the model learns that one video should be preferred over another rather than only learning isolated labels. At serving time, those experience scores promote high-quality but underexposed videos. The same scores also guide page-level optimization through reinforcement learning, where the system adjusts a whole result page rather than one clip in isolation.
mech: The mechanism begins with a search request and a set of candidate short videos produced by an existing retrieval or ranking system. For each candidate, the system gathers multimodal evidence: the abstract does not list every input, but the word multimodal supports using content signals beyond a single text field, such as visual content, captions, descriptions, or other video-associated information. In the first training stage, that evidence is turned into annotations that mark candidate quality or expected experience. A large language model helps produce these annotations because it can judge content meaning without needing that exact video to have many historical clicks. A supervised model is then fine-tuned on those annotations, so it learns to map content evidence to an experience score. In the second stage, candidates are compared in pairs. The model is not only told that a video has a score; it is trained to prefer one candidate over another when the evidence says the first should give a better user experience. This creates partial orderings, which are especially useful for ranking because search is about relative placement. At inference time, the trained scorer assigns experience scores to candidates. The reranker uses those scores to lift good but underexposed videos. Finally, page-level reinforcement learning uses the scores as guidance when arranging the broader result page.
math: The main mathematical idea is ranking under biased evidence. Ranking means turning many candidate videos into an order, where early positions matter more because users see them first. The usual numbers, such as clicks or consumption, are not pure quality measurements; they are entangled with exposure. A video cannot receive clicks if the system rarely shows it. The paper therefore introduces a second source of evidence: a learned estimate of user experience from content. Supervised fine-tuning is example-based learning: the model sees multimodal video evidence paired with quality annotations and changes its internal settings so similar evidence leads to similar judgments later. Pairwise preference optimization is comparison-based learning: instead of asking for an absolute perfect score, it asks which of two candidates should come first. That fits reranking because the final decision is relative. Reinforcement learning at the page level adds another idea: the system treats page arrangement as a sequence of choices and adjusts choices according to rewards tied to user experience and consumption metrics. The tradeoff is exploration versus exploitation. Exploitation favors videos with proven behavior; exploration gives underexposed videos a chance when content evidence says they may be good.
dots: This paper sits between information retrieval and recommender systems in the repo's current family map. Search papers share the problem of choosing a small useful set from a huge pile, while recommender papers share the problem of making selection faithful when clicks, item meaning, time, fairness, cost, and feedback loops all move at once. Here the object is a search result page of short videos, and the failure is not only relevance but exposure bias: the platform's old choices shape the evidence used for future choices. It also connects to multimodal ranking because the quality signal must come from more than one form of content evidence. It connects to language-model-assisted systems because the large language model supplies prior judgment when platform-specific behavior is sparse. Finally, it connects to fairness and long-tail discovery in a narrow sense: not demographic fairness from the abstract, but fairer exposure for quality videos that lack historical traffic.
ww: The mechanism should help because it breaks one link in the feedback loop. In the naive system, a video's score is strongly tied to whether it has already been shown enough to collect behavior. That means early exposure, catchy packaging, and accidental clicks can masquerade as quality. A content-based experience score gives the reranker a different kind of evidence. If a video is underexposed but its visual, textual, and other content signals resemble examples judged to provide good experience, it can be promoted before it has massive interaction history. Pairwise learning strengthens this because ranking depends on comparisons: the system learns the difference between two candidates that may both have weak behavior records. Page-level reinforcement learning matters because search results are consumed as a page, not as isolated videos. A single promoted item can change what users watch next and how the page feels. The approach works only insofar as the annotations and preference comparisons capture real experience better than sparse clicks alone, but that is exactly the gap the abstract identifies.
po: The payoff is a practical reranking layer for long-tail short-video search. According to the abstract, the method improves offline metrics including AUC, NDCG@K, and human preference judgment, which means it looks better both by numerical ranking checks and by human comparison. More importantly, an online A/B test covering 15% of traffic shows gains in user experience and consumption metrics. The claimed capability is not merely a higher benchmark score. It is the ability to promote high-quality but underexposed videos in live search, reducing the tendency for sparse behavior data to amplify clickbait and shallow content.
limits: Several assumptions have to hold. The large language model's judgments and the constructed annotations must line up with what Kuaishou users actually experience, not just with polished-looking content. The multimodal evidence must contain enough information to distinguish useful videos from shallow or manipulative ones. Pairwise preferences must be reliable enough that learned partial orderings do not encode the annotator's blind spots. The abstract reports offline improvements and an online A/B test, but the provided text is truncated after "conf", so it does not show detailed experiment design, effect sizes, guardrail metrics, or long-term outcomes. It also does not prove that promoted long-tail videos remain good after creators adapt to the scoring system.
